title: Charades
description: Act out a word or phrase without speaking while your team races to guess it.
materials: Paper slips and a pen, a hat or bowl
rules: Split into two teams and write down movie, book, or phrase ideas on slips of paper, folded up in a bowl. Teams alternate sending one actor to draw a slip and act it out silently for their own team within a time limit (60-90 seconds), using only gestures — no talking, mouthing words, or props. Standard signals apply (number of words, "sounds like", syllable count). Correct guesses within time win the point; unguessed slips go back in the bowl.
example: The slip says "Titanic." The actor mimes standing at the front of a ship with arms out, then mimes an iceberg collision — teammates shout guesses until someone lands on it.

title: Mystery Monster
description: Guess who's hiding under the blanket in disguise.
rules: Everyone except one player leaves the room. The remaining players hide themselves together under a blanket, arranging themselves into a bizarre, monster-like shape, then the group re-enters the room. The one player who stayed has to guess who's hiding underneath.

title: Last Letter, First Letter
description: Chain words together where each one starts with the last letter of the one before it.
rules: Each word must start with the last letter of the previous word. Players take turns quickly, keeping the chain going as fast as they can.
example: Apple → Elephant → Turtle → Egg → Goat...

title: One Minute Movie
description: Reenact an entire movie's plot in under sixty seconds.
rules: Players must reenact an entire movie's story in under one minute. At the end, one player has to guess which movie it was.

title: Air Draw
description: Draw a word in the air with your finger for others to guess.
rules: One player "draws" a secret word in the air using only their finger, with no pen or paper. The other player watches and tries to guess the word from the motion alone.

title: Yes, And
description: A group scene where every player must accept and build on whatever the last person said.
rules: Someone starts a scene with a simple statement about where they are or what is happening. Each next player must respond starting conceptually with "yes, and" — accepting what was just established and adding something new to it. No one is allowed to deny, block, or contradict what came before. Keep the scene going for a few minutes before wrapping up.
example: Player 1: "Wow, this rowboat is really taking on water." Player 2: "Yes, and I think it is because of the shark I stabbed earlier." Player 3: "Yes, and now the shark is going to be a issue too."

title: Fortunately / Unfortunately
description: Build a silly story by alternating good news and bad news.
rules: Players alternate starting sentences with "Fortunately..." and then "Unfortunately..." to build a silly, escalating story together.
example: "Fortunately, we found a treasure chest." "Unfortunately, it was guarded by a crocodile."

title: Movie Plot
description: Guess the movie from a vague plot description, one clue at a time.
rules: One player writes a brief plot summary of a movie without giving away the title, then reads it aloud. After each round of incorrect guesses, they add another clue until someone guesses the movie.

title: Emotional Rollercoaster
description: The same neutral scene gets replayed again and again, each time with a wildly different emotion.
rules: Two players act out a neutral, everyday scene while the rest of the group calls out random emotions for them to instantly switch between.

title: The Expert
description: One player improvises as the world's leading expert on a completely made-up topic.
rules: One player becomes an "expert" on a nonsense topic, like toaster psychology. The other players ask questions, and the expert must improvise increasingly confident, detailed answers.

title: Pictionary
description: Draw a secret word for your team to guess before the timer runs out — no letters or numbers allowed.
materials: Paper or whiteboard, markers, a timer, word list or slips
rules: Split into teams. One player from the drawing team picks a word and has 60-90 seconds to draw clues (no letters, numbers, or verbal hints) while their team shouts guesses. If the team guesses correctly before time is up, they score a point. Rotate the artist each round and alternate between teams.
example: The word is "volcano." The artist draws a triangle mountain with squiggly lines shooting out the top — teammates yell "mountain! eruption! volcano!"

title: 20 Questions
description: Guess the person, place, or thing someone is thinking of using only yes-or-no questions.
rules: One person thinks of a person, place, or thing. The other players ask yes/no questions to narrow it down in 20 turns or fewer. For an extra challenge, limit the game to a theme like movie characters or objects in the kitchen.

title: Knuckle Tattoos
description: Everyone get's fake knuckle tattoos to share with the group
rules: Everyone sits in a circle and writes a 4 or 5 letter word on the person's knuckles to the right knuckle of the person on your right and write on the left knuckle to the person to the left of you. Then you reveal what two word knuckle combination to the group. Tip: Right hand = first word. Left hand = second word.
example: Left knuckle reads: Baby. Right knuckle reads: Girl. The person puts their knuckles together to read: Baby Girl

title: I Think, I Feel, I Want, I Need
description: Build an increasingly absurd story by completing four escalating prompts.
rules: Players alternate completing the sentence starters "I Think...", "I Feel...", "I Want...", and "I Need..." to build an escalating, ridiculous story together, trying to make each other laugh.
example: "I Think... I need to go to the doctor after my plane crash." "I Feel... the doctor should write me a letter to get my plane ticket refunded." "I Want... to get my money back after losing my left arm in the crash." "I Need... the money to build my own plane to fly in the future."

title: Celebrity Interview
description: One player improvises as a celebrity while the others fire off questions as reporters.
rules: One player pretends to be a celebrity, real or made up. The other players act as reporters, asking silly or serious questions for the celebrity to improvise answers to.

title: Spoons
description: Collect four of a kind and race to grab a spoon before you get left without one.
materials: A standard deck of cards, spoons (one fewer than the number of players)
rules: Place spoons in the center, one fewer than the number of players. Deal four cards to each player. Everyone simultaneously picks up one extra card from a dealer-controlled draw and passes one card to their left, continuously, trying to collect four of a kind. As soon as any player gets four of a kind, they quietly grab a spoon — everyone else scrambles to grab a spoon too. The player left without one is out (or gets a letter, spelling S-P-O-O-N-S over multiple rounds before elimination). Remove a spoon each round and keep playing until one player remains.
example: You quietly collect four queens and slide a spoon off the table — a beat later the whole table is diving for the remaining spoons.

title: Draw What You Hear
description: Draw a scene from a description alone, without ever hearing its name.
rules: One player describes a scene out loud without naming it directly. Everyone else draws what they think is being described, based only on the description.

title: Go Fish
description: Collect matching sets of four by asking opponents for cards, or dive into the deck when they say no.
rules: Deal 5-7 cards to each player; the rest forms the draw pile ("the pond"). On your turn, ask a specific opponent for a rank you already hold at least one of ("Do you have any 7s?"). If they have it, they must hand over all cards of that rank and you go again. If not, they say "Go fish" and you draw from the pond. Collecting all four of a rank lets you lay that set down. First to lay down all their cards (or have the most sets when the pond runs out) wins.
example: You hold two 7s and ask an opponent for 7s. They hand over their one 7, completing your set of four, and you get to ask again.

title: Would You Rather
description: Answer absurd or tough hypothetical dilemmas and debate your reasoning with the group.
rules: One player reads a "Would you rather" question with two options. Everyone answers and explains their reasoning, and the group can debate or push back before moving to the next question. Rotate who reads the question.
example: "Would you rather be able to fly but only 3 feet off the ground, or be invisible but only when no one is looking?" Sparks immediate, heated debate.

title: Psychiatrist
description: One player questions the group to diagnose the secret behavior pattern everyone else has agreed on.
rules: One player leaves the room. The rest of the group agrees on a shared "symptom" — for example, everyone pretends to be the person to their right, or everyone answers as if they're a cat. The psychiatrist returns and asks questions, trying to diagnose the group's secret behavior pattern.

title: Gibberish Interpreter
description: One player speaks total gibberish while another "interprets" it into a real message.
rules: Treat gibberish as a foreign language. One player speaks entirely in made-up gibberish words, and another player acts as the interpreter, translating the nonsense into a real message for the audience or other players. More players means more gibberish speakers and interpreters making up increasingly ridiculous stories together.

title: Paper Airplane Distance
description: Fold and fly a paper airplane for maximum distance, one shot, no do-overs.
materials: Paper (one sheet per player), a tape measure or marked-off distance
rules: Give each player one sheet of paper and a strict fold-and-throw time limit (e.g. 3 minutes to fold, one single throw each from the same starting line). Mark where each plane lands and measure the distance from the throw line. Longest distance wins. No re-throws, no redesigns after the first throw.
example: A carefully folded dart-style plane sails past everyone else’s efforts and lands nearly a full room-length away.

title: Scene Switch
description: A scene where the actors' roles or emotions flip instantly on command.
rules: Two players perform a short improvised scene. When someone shouts "Switch," they instantly swap roles or emotions and keep the scene going.

title: Kings Cup
description: A card-by-card party game where every value in the deck triggers its own rule or challenge.
materials: A standard deck of cards, a cup or empty glass in the center
rules: Spread the deck face-down around a central cup and assign a rule or action to each card value before you start (for example: 2s point to someone who follows a rule, 7s means everyone reaches for the ceiling, Jacks are "never have I ever," Queens ask a question that gets passed around, and Kings add to a shared central pool). Take turns drawing a card and following whatever rule matches it. Keep going until all four Kings have been drawn.

title: Telephone Pictionary
description: A folded chain of alternating drawings and written guesses that gets delightfully wrong by the end.
rules: Each player writes a short phrase on the first page of their notepad, then passes it to the next player. That player draws a picture of the phrase (no peeking at earlier pages), folds the paper to hide everything but their drawing, and passes it on. The next player writes a guess of what the drawing shows based only on the picture, folds it, and passes it on. Keep alternating draw/guess until the notepads are full, then unfold each one and read the chain aloud from start to finish.
example: Starting phrase: "A cat riding a skateboard." Six passes later the final guess reads "A furry burrito on wheels."

title: 3 Words Pass
description: Write three clue words, pass them along, and watch a chain of drawings and guesses unfold.
rules: Write down three words: a descriptive word, a location, and a thing. Pass your three words to the next player, who draws them, then a different player tries to guess the original three words from the drawing.

title: Charades (Reverse)
description: The whole team acts out the clue together while one lone guesser tries to name it.
materials: Paper slips and a pen, a hat or bowl
rules: Same clue pool as regular charades, but flipped: one player is the guesser, and everyone else on the team acts out the clue together, at the same time, silently. The guesser watches the chaos and tries to shout the answer before time runs out. Rotate the guesser each round.
example: The clue is "Jurassic Park." The whole team scatters, some stomping like dinosaurs, others miming screaming and running — the guesser has to piece it together fast.

title: Exquisite Corpse
description: A collaborative drawing built in secret sections that only comes together at the reveal.
rules: Fold a sheet of paper into sections, one per player. Each player draws part of a figure (like a head) in their section without looking at what anyone else drew, then folds the paper to hide their part before passing it on, leaving just a small guideline showing. Keep passing and drawing until every section is filled, then unfold the paper to reveal the whole mismatched creature together.

title: Connect The Doodles
description: Turn a random squiggle into something recognizable.
rules: One player draws a random, meaningless squiggle. The next player has to build on it and turn it into something recognizable.

title: Freeze
description: Two players improvise a scene until someone freezes the action and jumps in with a new one.
rules: Two players start improvising a short scene. At any point, someone watching yells "Freeze!" — the two actors immediately stop moving, holding their exact positions. The person who called freeze taps one actor out, takes their exact physical position, and starts a brand new scene justified by that pose (it should have nothing to do with the scene before it). Keep going, swapping people in and out on freezes.
example: Two players are frozen mid-argument, one pointing at the other. A new player taps in, takes the pointing pose, and starts a scene as a tour guide pointing out a museum exhibit.

title: What Am I Thinking?
description: Ask yes-or-no questions to guess the simple concept someone is thinking of.
rules: The leader thinks of a simple concept, like the moon. The other players take turns asking only yes-or-no questions until someone guesses it.

title: Match Categories Team Game
description: A Taskmaster-inspired category game score points by matching your teammate without matching the other team.
rules: Split into teams of two. Someone names a category, and every player writes down 5 things that fit it, trying to think of things nobody else will write. An original answer (one nobody else wrote) is worth 1 point; matching your own teammate's answer is worth 2 points; but if your answer also matches the opposing team's, it cancels out and nobody scores for it. Play 12 rounds for a long game, 8 for a regular game, or 4 for a quick game, letting each player pick a category in turn. The team with the most points wins — there's no individual winner.
example: Category: "Things in a kitchen." You write "toaster" and your teammate also writes "toaster" — since nobody on the other team wrote it, you both score 2 points.

title: Mind Melt
description: Two players try to blurt out the exact same word at the same time. Beginner-friendly warm-up.
rules: Both players count down together, then simultaneously say any word that comes to mind. If the words don't match, count down and try again, letting each other's guesses influence you until you converge on the same word.
example: Round 1: one player says "ocean," the other says "sky." Round 2: one says "blue," the other says "water." Round 3: both say "wave!" at the same time.

title: Snort, Raspberry, Whistle
description: Race against the clock to chain together as many snorts, raspberries, and whistles as you can.
rules: In one minute, see how many times you can snort, blow a raspberry, and whistle in sequence, back to back. Whoever completes the most full sequences in the minute wins.

title: Contact
description: Guess a secret word before anyone else by trading clues with the group.
rules: The leader thinks of a word and says its first letter. The other players try to guess the word by giving clues to each other. If two players "make contact" by guessing the same word at the same time, the leader must reveal the next letter. Be the first to guess the secret word.

title: Slide Show
description: A group freezes into a series of "photo slides" while two narrators improvise the story behind them.
rules: Works best with three to six slide-show players and two narrators. Ask the audience for a suggestion, like a vacation destination. The slide-show players freeze into a physical pose for each "slide," and the two narrators improvise a story describing what's happening in the picture. When the narrators say "Click," the players snap into a new pose for the next slide, and the narrators keep building the story. A great option for kids or players who are shy about speaking.
example: "Oh Bob, remember when the black bear attacked little Trudy?" "Yes, and all you had was one bandaid on the floor of the car..." Click. "Oh Nancy, this is when we went to the state fair..."

title: Tallest Tower
description: Build the tallest freestanding tower using only what is already on the table, against the clock.
materials: Whatever is on the table (cups, books, utensils, etc.), a timer
rules: Give everyone 2 minutes and free rein over whatever is within reach on the table (no outside items). At "go," everyone builds the tallest freestanding structure they can. When time is up, hands off — no touching to keep it standing. Measure each tower; if one collapses during measurement, it is scored at its last stable height. Tallest standing tower wins.
example: One player stacks books into a pyramid topped with a precariously balanced spoon for extra height, and it holds just long enough to be measured.

title: Draw On Back Draw On Paper
description: A picture travels from paper to fingertip to paper again, changing a little each time.
rules: Sit in a line facing the same direction. The first player looks at a simple picture, then draws it with their finger on the back of the next player — no ink, just the motion. That player then draws what they felt onto a fresh sheet of paper without seeing the original, then draws their version onto the back of the next player, and so on down the line. Compare the final paper drawing to the original at the end.

title: Who Am I?
description: Guess the famous person, character, or thing written on a card stuck to your forehead using only yes-or-no questions.
rules: Write the name of a famous person, character, or thing on a card without letting the other player see it, then stick it to their forehead or hold it above their head. Take turns asking yes-or-no questions about the card you're wearing to figure out who or what you are.

title: Fishbowl (aka Salad Bowl)
description: The same set of clues, guessed three different ways across three rounds.
rules: Write down random nouns — famous people, objects, and more — on slips of paper and put them in a bowl. Split into teams and play three rounds using the same slips: Round 1, describe the word without saying it; Round 2, use only one word as a clue; Round 3, act it out like charades. Try to guess as many as possible each round.

title: Two Truths and a Lie
description: Everyone shares three personal statements — two true, one false — and the group votes on the lie.
rules: Each player in turn says three statements about themselves: two true facts and one made-up lie, in any order. The rest of the group discusses and votes on which statement they believe is the lie. The player then reveals the truth. Rotate until everyone has gone.
example: "I have run a marathon. I have met a celebrity. I am afraid of birds." The group debates, votes on the marathon claim, and finds out the celebrity meeting was the lie.

title: Two or Three Headed Interview
description: Two or three players share one body and one brain, answering interview questions in unison.
rules: Two or three players act as a single expert with multiple heads. An interviewer asks them questions, and they must answer in unison or by alternating words, creating comedic chaos while revealing their outlandish expertise.

title: One Word Story
description: Build a collaborative story one word at a time, with no idea where it’s going.
rules: Players take turns adding one word at a time to build a story together, creating unexpected twists and hilarious turns along the way. Nobody knows where the story is headed until it gets there.
example: Player 1: "The" → Player 2: "dragon" → Player 3: "ordered" → Player 1: "a" → Player 2: "pizza" → Player 3: "but..." — the story keeps building one word at a time.

title: Half Life
description: Improvise a scene, then compress it into shorter and shorter retellings.
rules: Improvise a short scene, then repeat it again in half the time, highlighting only the essential elements. Keep repeating and halving the time with each iteration, refining the story down to its core each round.
